## Origin

Rage Comics are short, crudely drawn stories assembled from reusable faces that represent emotions, personalities and punchlines. A creator could place Rage Guy, Trollface, Me Gusta, Forever Alone or Y U NO into a few boxes and rely on readers to understand the cast before reading the captions. The rough MS Paint look was part of the language, not a production flaw.

The first supported strip appeared anonymously on 4chan’s /b/ board in August 2008. Across four panels, a person sits on a toilet, experiences splashback and ends with a zoomed-in screaming face beside “FFFFFFFFUUUUUUUU—”. Reposts turned that final Rage Guy into a template, while new artists supplied other faces for different situations. Because the poster was anonymous, the exact calendar day is not responsibly known; MemePulse records August 2008 as the supported month.

The family expanded quickly but did not come from one author. Carlos Ramirez, using Whynne on DeviantArt, drew Trollface in September 2008 for a comic about pointless trolling on 4chan. Other characters came from manga panels, reaction drawings and independent webcomics before being absorbed into a shared library. Their different origins explain why the set never had one consistent drawing style.

## Spread

Reddit turned the library into an everyday storytelling system. The r/fffffffuuuuuuuuuuuu community—often shortened to f7u12—hosted stories about school, dating, parents, computers and tiny domestic failures. Online generators lowered the barrier further: users selected panels and faces, added captions, and published without drawing anything from scratch.

The comics developed their own grammar. “Le” introduced actions, “derp” named generic people, and familiar faces acted like stage directions. Rage Guy marked explosive frustration; Trollface announced deliberate provocation; Forever Alone made loneliness the punchline; Me Gusta signaled an unsettling pleasure. Readers learned this vocabulary by seeing it repeated.

By 2011 and 2012, rage faces had moved beyond image boards into Facebook stickers, merchandise, advertising, classrooms and live-action parody videos. Ars Technica described them as a standardized form of online communication, while The New York Times published a guide to turning daily stress into a comic. Search interest for Rage Guy, Rage Comics and Trollface peaked around February 2012.

The boom faded as generator sites filled with repetitive submissions and newer formats offered fresher voices. Yet the faces did not disappear. Trollface remained a general symbol of trolling; Y U NO survived as an image macro; reaction faces returned through ironic nostalgia, redraws and “meme renaissance” communities.

Rage Comics mattered because they separated storytelling from drawing skill. They gave millions of people a common cast, emotional shorthand and a four-panel stage for small personal stories. Later Wojak comics, starter packs and reusable character ecosystems follow the same basic idea: shared figures make a private experience instantly legible to strangers.

results.description: One of the most widely used rage comic faces is the Trollface, drawn by Oakland artist Carlos Ramirez in 2008. Originally posted in a comic to his DeviantArt account Whynne about Internet trolling on 4chan, the trollface is a recognizable image of Internet memes and culture.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

An example of a rage comic

A **rage comic** is a short [cartoon strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webcomic 'Webcomic') using a growing set of pre-made cartoon faces, or **rage faces**, which usually express [rage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_(emotion) 'Rage (emotion)') or some other simple emotion or activity.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-1) They are usually crudely drawn in [Microsoft Paint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Paint 'Microsoft Paint') or other simple drawing programs, and were most popular in the early 2010s.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-:0-2) These [webcomics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webcomic 'Webcomic') have spread much in the same way that [Internet memes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme 'Internet meme') do, and several memes have originated in this medium. They have been characterized by _[Ars Technica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars_Technica 'Ars Technica')_ as an "accepted and standardized form of online communication".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-ars-3) The popularity of rage comics has been attributed to their use as vehicles for humorizing shared experiences.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-4)

## History

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rage_comic&action=edit&section=1 'Edit section: History')\]

T-shirts featuring internet meme rage comics, seen in 2013, at their height.

See also: [Trollface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trollface 'Trollface')

A man [cosplaying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosplay 'Cosplay') as Rage Guy at [Anime Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime_Los_Angeles 'Anime Los Angeles') 2012

Although used on numerous websites such as [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit 'Reddit'), [Cheezburger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheezburger 'Cheezburger'), ESS.MX, Ragestache, and [9GAG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9GAG '9GAG'), the source of the rage comic has largely been attributed to [4chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4chan '4chan') in mid-2008. The first rage comic was posted to the 4chan /b/ "Random" board in 2008. It was a simple 4-panel strip showing the author's anger about having water splash into their anus while on the toilet, with the final panel featuring a zoomed-in face, known as Rage Guy, saying "FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUU-". It was quickly reposted and modified, with other users creating new scenarios and characters.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-weirdworm-5)\[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources 'Wikipedia:Verifiability')_\]

Google Trends data shows that the term "rage guy" peaked in February 2012 while the terms "rage comics" and "troll face" both peaked at the same time.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-:0-2) The range of expression and standardized, easily identifiable faces has allowed uses such as [teaching English as a foreign language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teaching_English_as_a_foreign_language 'Teaching English as a foreign language').[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-english-6)

One of the most widely used rage comic faces is the [Trollface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trollface 'Trollface'), drawn by [Oakland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland,_California 'Oakland, California') artist Carlos Ramirez in 2008.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-:1-7) Originally posted in a comic to his [DeviantArt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeviantArt 'DeviantArt') account Whynne about [Internet trolling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_trolling 'Internet trolling') on 4chan,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-8) the trollface is a recognizable image of Internet memes and [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberculture 'Cyberculture'). Ramirez has used his creation, registered with the [United States Copyright Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Copyright_Office 'United States Copyright Office') in 2010, to gain over $100,000 in licensing fees, settlements, and other payouts.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-:1-7) The video game _[Meme Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meme_Run 'Meme Run')_ for [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo 'Nintendo')'s [Wii U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_U 'Wii U') console was taken down for having the trollface as the main character.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-:1-7)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-10)

Another character that is frequently used in rage comics is the "Y U NO" (shorthand for "why you no"[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-Dictionary.com_2018-03-01-11)) guy, a character with a big round head, deep [wrinkles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrinkle 'Wrinkle'), thin arms and a look of intense [annoyance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annoyance 'Annoyance'). He is also often used in [image macro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_macro 'Image macro') form.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-Ars_Technica_2012-03-10-12) He was used on a [billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard 'Billboard') on [the 101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_101 'U.S. Route 101') to advertise a chat platform in 2011[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-TechCrunch_2011-04-23-13) and on the cover of [_The Gap_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gap_(magazine) 'The Gap (magazine)') in 2012.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-thegap2012-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-Yahoo_Finance_2013-06-28-15)

In China, rage comics are known as _Bàozǒu Mànhuà_ ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters 'Traditional Chinese characters'): 暴走漫画), shortened to _Baoman_ ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters 'Traditional Chinese characters'): 暴漫). They contain many of the same characters as Western rage comics but also contain original characters. _Baoman_ gained widespread online popularity in China when artist Wang Nima created the website baozoumanhua.com. By 2012, the website received between 5000 and 8000 daily comic submissions. In 2018, the website was banned because creator Wang Nima made jokes about Chinese military heroes such as [Ye Ting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ye_Ting 'Ye Ting') and [Dong Cunrui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dong_Cunrui 'Dong Cunrui'). The social media site [Weibo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibo 'Weibo') also terminated 16 accounts related to rage comics.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-16) In 2018, [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix 'Netflix') released the film _[Next Gen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next_Gen_(film) 'Next Gen (film)')_, which is an adaptation of one of Wang Nima's rage comics titled _7723_.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_comic#cite_note-17)
